column2: Normal physiology: a virtual laboratory based on 15 lab exercises — step-by-step work with instruments, measuring, calculating and evaluating the result

15 virtual cases based on the laboratory exercises in the normal physiology manual. In each one you work step by step with the instruments, measure, calculate and evaluate the result. If the sequence is violated or a step is done incorrectly, it is recorded as an error in the laboratory notebook.
Fill in all fields and select a conclusion
(each one lowers the result by 8 %, by 50 % at most)
Stimulation threshold and the law of strength

Object: a frog nerve–muscle preparation (sciatic nerve + gastrocnemius muscle). Task: by stimulating the nerve indirectly and the muscle directly, determine their stimulation thresholds and the maximal stimulus strength for stimulation through the nerve, and demonstrate the law of strength.
Fix the preparation in the clamp and connect its tendon to the myograph lever
Moisten the preparation with Ringer's solution
Place the electrodes on the sciatic nerve (indirect stimulation)
Slowly raise the voltage from zero to find the threshold of the nerve
Raise the strength to show the maximal contraction and that the amplitude does not grow at supramaximal strength
Move the electrodes to the muscle and raise the voltage from zero to find the threshold of the muscle
Kymogram (single twitches; the drum is advanced by hand; 1 mm = 4 px)
The preparation was fixed in the clamp and its tendon was connected to the lever with a thread.
The preparation was moistened with Ringer's solution.
First determine the threshold and maximal strength through the nerve (steps 3–5)
The electrodes were placed on the sciatic nerve.
Needle electrodes were inserted into the muscle (direct stimulation).
The electrodes are not placed on the preparation
The preparation is not moistened with Ringer's solution — it dries quickly and loses its excitability
Note: moisten the preparation with Ringer's solution from time to time so that it does not dry out.
A new sheet of paper was placed on the kymograph drum.
To determine the threshold, the voltage had to be raised slowly starting from zero (from subthreshold values)
On the electrostimulator, «−/+» changes the voltage by 0.05 V and «« »» by 0.5 V. After each stimulus the drum is advanced slightly by hand; the voltage is written below.
Maximal stimulus strength for stimulation through the nerve
V (a stronger stimulus does not increase the amplitude)
Conclusion: what do the results show?

The threshold of the nerve is low — its excitability is higher than that of the muscle; the amplitude increases from threshold to maximum because more and more muscle fibers are excited (law of strength)
The threshold of the muscle is low — its excitability is higher than that of the nerve; the increase in amplitude depends on the contraction force of each fiber increasing
The whole muscle obeys the "all-or-none" law, so the amplitude does not depend on strength
The higher the threshold, the higher the excitability

Excitability is inversely proportional to the threshold strength: the threshold of the nerve is low, so its excitability is high. The whole muscle consists of fibers with different thresholds — as the strength increases, the number of excited fibers grows (law of strength). At maximal strength all fibers are excited; supramaximal strength does not increase the amplitude. An individual fiber, however, obeys the "all-or-none" law.
In this preparation: the threshold of the nerve is ⟦0⟧ V and the maximal strength is ⟦1⟧ V; the threshold of the muscle is ⟦2⟧ V (≈ ⟦3⟧ times higher than that of the nerve).
Phases of contraction, unfused and fused tetanus, optimum and pessimum

Object: a frog nerve–muscle preparation, myograph, kymograph, time marker (100 Hz — each tooth is 10 ms). Task: measure the phases of a single twitch, record unfused and fused tetanus by stimulating at different frequencies, and demonstrate pessimum.
Mount the preparation and moisten it with Ringer's solution
Set the drum to «fast» speed and record a single twitch with one stimulus
Switch the drum to «slow» speed and record unfused tetanus at a low frequency (2 s)
Increase the frequency and record fused tetanus
Show pessimum at 100 Hz and above, then show recovery of the contraction (optimum) by lowering the frequency
The preparation was mounted and moistened with Ringer's solution. The electrodes are on the nerve.
Mount and moisten the preparation first
On a slow drum a single twitch is recorded as a thin line — the phases cannot be measured. The «fast» speed is needed for the phases.
Tetanus cannot be recorded on a fast-rotating drum — in 2 s the tape moves more than 1 m. Choose the «slow» speed.
a series of separate single twitches
a short rise at the beginning, then the contraction drops sharply

Lower lines: stimulus marker and time marker. On the «fast» drum each wave of the time marker is 10 ms; count the latent period from the stimulus mark until the curve begins to rise, the contraction phase up to the peak, and the relaxation until it returns to the baseline.
You did not record at ⟦0⟧ Hz. ⟦1⟧ tetanus in this preparation: ⟦2⟧ Hz
Frequency at which unfused tetanus was recorded
Frequency at which fused tetanus was recorded
When each subsequent stimulus falls in the contraction phase of the previous contraction
When each subsequent stimulus falls in the relaxation phase of the previous contraction
When the interval between stimuli is longer than the duration of a single twitch
When the impulses fall in the absolute refractory period of the muscle

If a stimulus falls in the relaxation phase of the previous contraction, unfused tetanus results; if it falls in the contraction phase, the contractions summate completely and fused tetanus results. The amplitude of tetanus is greater than that of a single twitch. At a very high frequency (above 100 Hz) the impulses exceed the lability of the neuromuscular synapse — pessimum; when the frequency is reduced, the contraction recovers (optimum).
In this preparation: latent period ⟦0⟧ ms, contraction ⟦1⟧ ms, relaxation ⟦2⟧ ms (single twitch ≈ ⟦3⟧ ms). By frequency: ⟦4⟧.
Determination of rheobase and chronaxie with an electronic chronaxiemeter

Subject: a 34-year-old man who, 2 months after a humerus fracture, has difficulty extending his wrist (injury of the radial nerve is suspected). Task: determine the rheobase and chronaxie at the motor point of the wrist extensor muscles.
Subject: a healthy 20-year-old student. Task: determine the rheobase and chronaxie at the motor point of the forearm ⟦0⟧ muscles with an electronic chronaxiemeter.
Moisten the skin area with physiological saline
Place the passive (indifferent) electrode on the scapular region
Place the active electrode on the motor point of the muscle
With long impulses (≥ 100 ms), slowly raise the voltage to find the rheobase
Set the voltage to double the rheobase
Reduce the impulse duration to find the shortest time that still causes a contraction (chronaxie)
The skin was moistened (contact resistance decreases).
The passive electrode was placed over the scapula.
The active electrode was placed on the motor point.
The skin is not moistened — the result will be incorrect
The voltage had to be raised slowly starting from zero (from a value that causes no contraction)

The chronaxiemeter delivers rectangular impulses. An impulse of 100 ms or longer acts practically like a direct current — the rheobase is determined in this mode. The voltage step is 0.5 V; the duration is reduced in steps of 0.01 ms.
Chronaxie is within the normal range — muscle excitability is normal
Chronaxie is sharply increased — excitability is reduced, typical of nerve injury
Chronaxie is decreased — excitability is reduced
Chronaxie cannot be evaluated because the rheobase is high

Chronaxie is the shortest time a current equal to twice the rheobase needs to cause excitation; it is a measure of excitability in terms of time: the smaller the chronaxie, the higher the excitability. Normally it is 0.08–0.16 ms in flexor muscles and 0.16–0.32 ms in extensors. When a nerve is injured, the chronaxie of the muscle increases tens of times; with recovery it returns to normal.
In this subject the rheobase is ⟦0⟧ V and the chronaxie is ⟦1⟧ ms. Threshold formula (Weiss–Lapicque): U = Rb·(1 + chr/t); when t = chr, U = 2·Rb.
Counting red blood cells in the Goryaev chamber
complains of weakness, fatigue and dizziness
a mountaineer who has lived for 3 months at a mountain base at 3500 m altitude
Subject: ⟦0⟧-year-old ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧. Task: determine the number of red blood cells in capillary blood using the Goryaev chamber.
Pour 4 ml of 3 % NaCl solution into a test tube
Wipe the finger with alcohol and prick it; wipe away the first drop with cotton
Take 0.02 ml of blood, add it to the test tube and mix (1 : 200)
Cover the Goryaev chamber with the cover glass (until Newton's rings appear)
Fill the chamber with the diluted blood and wait 1 minute
Under the microscope (×8), count the red blood cells in the 1st large square according to Egorov's rule
Add the results of the other 4 large squares and calculate the number of red blood cells
4 ml of 3 % NaCl was poured into the test tube.
The fingertip was wiped with alcohol.
The finger must be wiped with alcohol before pricking (asepsis)
The finger was pricked and a drop of blood appeared.
Wipe away the 1st drop with cotton
The first drop was wiped away (it is mixed with tissue fluid).
Take 0.02 ml of blood → test tube
The finger has not been pricked
The first drop was not wiped away — it contains tissue fluid, so the result will be low
0.02 ml of blood was taken, the outside of the pipette was wiped and the blood was blown into the test tube.
There is no blood in the test tube yet
The cover glass was slid on with friction — Newton's rings are visible.
Dilute and mix the blood first
The chamber must first be covered with the cover glass — otherwise the chamber depth (0.1 mm) is disturbed
The chamber was filled. Wait 1 minute for the red blood cells to settle.
Only ⟦0⟧ s have passed — the red blood cells have not settled; they float at different focal planes

The 1st large square (16 small squares) is in the field of view. Mark each red blood cell you count by clicking it (click again to remove the mark). Egorov's rule: cells inside the square and on the upper and left lines are counted; cells on the lower and right lines are not.
Red blood cells you counted in the 1st large square: ⟦0⟧.
Your colleague counted squares 2–5 diagonally. Now calculate the total number (A) and the red blood cell count: X = A × 4000 × 200 / 80 (per µL).
Number of red blood cells in the 1st large square (by Egorov's rule)
Total in the 5 large squares (80 small squares), A
The red blood cell count is normal
The red blood cell count is decreased (erythropenia, typical of anemia)
The red blood cell count is increased (erythrocytosis)
Normal: 4.0–5.0 in men and 3.7–4.7 in women × 10¹²/L. At high altitude, hypoxia increases the production of erythropoietin in the kidney — absolute erythrocytosis develops.

In the microscope image: green ring — counted correctly, yellow broken ring — missed (⟦0⟧), red × — a cell that should not have been counted (on the lower/right line or outside) (⟦1⟧). Formula: X = A × 4000 × 200 / 80 = A × 10 000 (per µL), i.e. A/100 × 10¹²/L.
Hemoglobin and color index by the Sahli method
Sahli hemometer, acid hematin, calculating the color index
complains of heavy menstrual bleeding, weakness and hair loss
after gastric resection; has a burning tongue and numbness in the legs
Subject: ⟦0⟧-year-old ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧. Red blood cell count on the laboratory form: ⟦3⟧ × 10¹²/L. Task: determine the hemoglobin level by the Sahli method and calculate the color index.
Pour 0.1 N HCl into the middle test tube of the hemometer up to the lower mark (2)
Wipe the finger with alcohol and prick it; wipe away the first drop
Take 20 µL (0.02 ml) of blood, wipe the pipette tip, blow the blood into the HCl and mix
Add distilled water drop by drop and match the color to the standards
Read the hemoglobin level from the scale
0.1 N HCl was poured into the middle test tube up to the «2» mark.
The finger was wiped with alcohol.
The finger must be wiped with alcohol before pricking
The first drop was wiped away with cotton.
There is no HCl in the test tube yet
The first drop was not wiped away
20 µL of blood was taken, the pipette tip was wiped, the blood was blown into the HCl and the pipette was rinsed with HCl. The stopwatch was started.
Only ⟦0⟧ have passed — acid hematin has not formed completely (the color is still pale). Water is added after 5 minutes; otherwise the result will be low.
The test tube is much darker than the standards
The test tube is slightly darker than the standards
The test tube is lighter than the standards — too much water was added
Too much water was added: the color is lighter than the standard. In this case the hemoglobin comes out higher than the true value; to get an accurate result the analysis must be restarted.
The colors have not been matched yet
Read from the lower edge of the meniscus (magnified view on the right).
Compare the color against a white background in daylight, placing the test tubes side by side. Add the water one drop at a time at the end: water added in excess cannot be taken back.
Color index (CI = Hb, g/L × 3 / first 3 digits of the red blood cell count)
Conclusion based on the color index:

The CI shows the relative saturation of a single red blood cell with hemoglobin. In iron deficiency the red blood cells are small and pale (hypochromic), whereas in vitamin B₁₂ and folic acid deficiency they are large and saturated with hemoglobin (megalocytes) — hyperchromia. The Sahli method is subjective, with an error of up to ± 10 %.
True hemoglobin ⟦0⟧ g/L; red blood cells ⟦1⟧ × 10¹²/L; CI = ⟦2⟧. Normal: 130–160 g/L in men, 120–140 g/L in women.
Sodium citrate, capillary, 1 hour, plasma column
fever, cough and chest pain for 5 days (pneumonia is suspected)
Subject: ⟦0⟧-year-old ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧. Task: determine the erythrocyte sedimentation rate by the Panchenkov method.
Rinse the capillary with 5 % sodium citrate solution
Draw citrate up to the «P» mark (50) and expel it onto a watch glass
Draw blood from the finger up to the «K» mark twice and add it to the citrate (4 : 1)
Mix, then draw the mixture into the capillary up to the «K» (0) mark
Place the capillary upright in the stand and note the time
After 1 hour measure the height of the plasma column
The capillary was rinsed with 5 % sodium citrate.
Draw citrate up to «P» and expel it onto the glass
50 divisions of citrate were expelled onto the watch glass.
Draw blood up to «K» and add it to the glass
Blood was drawn up to the «K» mark ⟦0⟧ times and added to the watch glass.
Too much blood was added — the blood-to-citrate ratio of 4 : 1 is disturbed
Mix and draw into the capillary up to «K»
Blood was drawn only once — it must be drawn twice to give a 4 : 1 ratio
Blood has not been added yet
The mixture was drawn up to the «K» (0) mark without air bubbles.
There is no mixture in the capillary
The capillary was placed upright and the timer was started.
The capillary is not placed in the stand
Only ⟦0⟧ minutes have passed — ESR is measured at 1 hour
The measurement was delayed (⟦0⟧ minutes) — the red blood cells keep settling, so the result will be too high
Read the plasma column in mm on the magnified scale.

Magnified view of the capillary: scale 0–100 mm. At the top is clear yellow plasma, at the bottom the settled red blood cells. ESR is the height of the plasma column after 1 hour (mm/h). The timer stops by itself at 60 minutes.
ESR is increased — typical of an inflammatory process (nonspecific sign)
ESR is increased for a physiological reason (pregnancy)

Normal: 1–10 mm/h in men and 2–15 mm/h in women. When fibrinogen and globulins increase, red blood cells form «rouleaux» and settle faster: in inflammation (pathological) and in the second half of pregnancy (physiological, up to 40–50 mm/h). ESR is a nonspecific indicator — it does not establish a diagnosis.
In this subject the ESR is ⟦0⟧ mm/h.
Determining blood group and Rh factor
Anti-A, anti-B and anti-D Zoliclones (monoclonal reagents); evaluating agglutination
Subject: a patient preparing for elective surgery. Task: determine the ABO blood group and Rh factor using Zoliclones.
Label the plate: anti-A, anti-B, anti-D
Add 1 drop (0.1 ml) of the corresponding Zoliclone to each mark
Take blood from the finger and place a drop 10 times smaller next to each drop
Mix each drop with a separate clean stick
Rock the plate slowly and observe: anti-A, anti-B — 2.5 minutes, anti-D — 3 minutes
Read the result (if there is agglutination with both Zoliclones — control with physiological saline)
blood (on the tip of the stick)
First label the plate (which reagent goes where)
First select an instrument or reagent
Wrong reagent: ⟦1⟧ was dropped on the spot marked «⟦0⟧»
First add the reagent, then place the blood next to it
A small drop of blood was placed next to ⟦0⟧.
There is no blood in this spot yet
⟦0⟧: mixed with a new clean stick.
The plate is being rocked slowly.
The 4th spot was marked for control: physiological saline + blood + mixing.
The three spots are not fully prepared
Only ⟦0⟧ s have passed — the result is evaluated after 2.5 minutes (anti-D after 3 minutes); weak agglutination appears late
The plate was not rocked — agglutination will be weak and may be missed
Control (saline): no agglutination — the result is reliable.
Instrument in hand (then click a spot on the plate)
In blood group AB (IV) (agglutination with both Zoliclones) the control test with physiological saline was not performed
What does agglutination with a Zoliclone mean?
The corresponding agglutinogen (antigen) is present on the red blood cells
The corresponding agglutinin (antibody) is present in the plasma
The blood clotting system has been activated
Hemolysis of the red blood cells

Zoliclones are monoclonal antibodies; they directly detect the antigen (agglutinogen) on the red blood cell membrane: agglutination with anti-A means antigen A is present, with anti-B antigen B, and with anti-D antigen D (Rh). If agglutination occurs with both Zoliclones (group AB), a control with physiological saline is run to exclude false agglutination.
Filter paper, stopwatch, tilting the capillary
pinpoint hemorrhages under the skin and bleeding gums over the last month; platelets 38 × 10⁹/L
prolonged bleeding after minor injuries since childhood, bleeding into the knee joint (his mother's brother has the same disease)
Subject: ⟦0⟧. Task: determine the bleeding time by the Duke method and the clotting time of capillary blood by the Sukharev method.
Wipe the earlobe with alcohol and let it dry
Puncture to a depth of 3–4 mm with a scarifier and start the stopwatch
Every 30 seconds blot the drop of blood with filter paper (without touching the skin)
Mark the time when no spot is left on the paper
Draw 25–30 mm of blood from the finger into a Sukharev capillary and start the stopwatch
Tilt the capillary every 30 seconds to find the beginning and the end of clotting
The earlobe was wiped with alcohol.
The skin was dried (if alcohol remains, the blood spreads and does not form a drop).
Punctured and the stopwatch started. A drop of blood is coming out by itself (do not squeeze!).
Interval ⟦0⟧ s — the drop must be blotted every 30 seconds
First blotting at ⟦0⟧ s — it should be at 30 seconds
⟦0⟧ — a spot remained on the paper.
⟦0⟧ — no spot remained: the bleeding has stopped.
Draw blood from the finger into the capillary + stopwatch
The finger was wiped and pricked, the first drop was wiped away; 25–30 mm of blood was drawn into the capillary and the stopwatch was started.
No blood has been drawn into the capillary
The capillary is being tilted too often — tilt it every 30 seconds
the blood column moves slowly, with difficulty — clotting has begun
the blood column does not move, fibrin threads are visible in the capillary — clotting is complete

Duke: the paper touches the drop but must not touch the skin wound — otherwise the clot is damaged. Sukharev: the beginning of clotting is the time when the movement of the column slows down; the end is the time when the column stops completely.
Bleeding and clotting times are normal — hemostasis is not impaired
Bleeding time is prolonged, clotting time is normal — vascular-platelet hemostasis is impaired
Clotting time is prolonged, bleeding time is normal — coagulation hemostasis is impaired

The Duke method assesses vascular-platelet (primary) hemostasis — normal 2–4 minutes; it is prolonged in thrombocytopenia. Capillary blood clotting (Sukharev): beginning 30 s – 2 minutes, end 3–5 minutes; it is prolonged in clotting-factor deficiency (hemophilia), while the bleeding time remains normal.
In this subject: bleeding stopped at ⟦0⟧; clotting began at ⟦1⟧ and ended at ⟦2⟧ (accuracy ± 30 s with 30-second tilting).
There is air in the cuff — release the air first
The cuff covers the elbow crease — the stethoscope cannot be placed; the cuff is tied 2–2.5 cm above the elbow
The cuff was tied on the arm 2–2.5 cm above the elbow, so that one finger fits under it.
The stethoscope was placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa.
The valve is open — first close the valve, otherwise the air will escape
The cuff was inflated only to ⟦0⟧ mm — this is below the systolic pressure; the sounds are heard immediately and the systolic pressure cannot be determined
The cuff was inflated unnecessarily high — it causes pain to the patient (20–30 mm above the point where the pulse disappears is enough)
Note: after the pulse disappears, inflating a further 20–30 mm is recommended (so as not to miss the auscultatory gap).
While inflating, you did not monitor the radial pulse by palpation (you need to know the pressure at which the pulse disappears)
The air is being released too fast (> 4 mm/s) — the pressure falls too much between sounds, so the result will be inaccurate
The stethoscope was not placed — no sounds were heard
No sounds were heard — repeat the measurement.
anterior axillary line, at the level of V4
midaxillary line, at the level of V4
Placing electrodes, calibration, measuring intervals in lead II
19-year-old student, excited before an exam, has drunk 2 cups of coffee
Subject: ⟦0⟧. Task: record an ECG with correctly placed electrodes, measure the RR, PQ, QRS and QT intervals and the R wave amplitude in standard lead II, and evaluate the heart rate and rhythm.
Lay the subject down, wipe the electrode sites with alcohol and apply gel
Place the limb electrodes according to color
Place the chest electrodes at points V1–V6
Calibrate (1 mV = 10 mm) and choose the paper speed
Measure the intervals and amplitude with calipers in lead II
First wipe the skin with alcohol and apply gel
A limb electrode is placed here
A chest electrode is placed here
The skin was wiped with alcohol and gel was applied to the electrode sites.
Note: the standard gain is 10 mm/mV. With any other value the amplitude will have to be recalculated.
Select an electrode, then click a point on the body
The limb electrodes are not all placed
No calibration signal was given before recording — the amplitude cannot be evaluated
The ⟦0⟧ electrode is in the wrong place (⟦1⟧); the correct place is ⟦2⟧
The chest electrodes are not all placed
Attention: in lead I the P wave and QRS came out negative.
Paper speed ⟦0⟧ mm/s (1 mm = ⟦1⟧ s), gain ⟦2⟧ mm/mV. Drag the caliper lines over the strip; the interval is shown in mm. A small square is 1 mm, a large square is 5 mm.
R wave amplitude in lead II
The rhythm does not originate from the sinus node (no P wave)

Criteria of sinus rhythm: in lead II the P wave is positive and precedes every QRS, the PQ is constant and the RR intervals are equal. In athletes vagal tone is high — physiological sinus bradycardia; excitement and caffeine cause sinus tachycardia through sympathetic influence. Norms: PQ 0.12–0.20 s, QRS 0.06–0.10 s, QT depends on heart rate (approximately 0.36–0.44 s).
In this recording: HR ⟦0⟧, RR ⟦1⟧ s, P ⟦2⟧ s, PQ ⟦3⟧ s, QRS ⟦4⟧ s, QT ⟦5⟧ s, R (II) ⟦6⟧ mV.⟦7⟧
Because the arm electrodes were swapped, lead I is inverted and leads II and III have exchanged places.
Measuring arterial blood pressure by the Korotkoff method
56-year-old man, pain in the occipital region, «floaters» before the eyes
Subject: ⟦0⟧; sat quietly for 5 minutes, arm at heart level, palm facing up. Task: measure arterial blood pressure by the Korotkoff method and calculate the pulse pressure and mean arterial pressure.
Tie the cuff on the arm 2–2.5 cm above the elbow
Place the stethoscope over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa
Palpate the radial pulse and inflate until the pulse disappears and a further 20–30 mm
Open the valve and release the air slowly (2–3 mm/s)
Mark the pressure at the first sound (systolic) and at the disappearance of sounds (diastolic)
The measurement is finished. Enter what the manometer showed at the first and the last sounds you heard. If needed, you can repeat the measurement after 2–3 minutes.

Hold down the «Inflate» button and watch the manometer needle. When you move the valve to the «slow» position the air escapes at 2–3 mm/s. The sounds are heard in the stethoscope (turn the sound on); a «TAP» sign also appears on the screen.

Systolic pressure is the pressure at which the first clear Korotkoff sound appears (blood begins to pass through the compressed artery with turbulent flow); diastolic is the pressure at which the sounds disappear completely (the artery is fully open, flow is laminar). Normal pulse pressure is 40–50 and mean arterial pressure is ≈ 80–95 mm Hg.
In your measurement the first sound was heard at ≈ ⟦0⟧ and the last at ≈ ⟦1⟧ mm Hg.
20 squats: pulse and pressure response, recovery

Subject: ⟦0⟧-year-old student. Task: measure pulse and arterial blood pressure at rest, after 20 squats and at the end of the 3rd minute, and determine the type of cardiovascular response to exercise.
Count the pulse for 10 s at rest
Measure arterial blood pressure at rest
Count the pulse for 10 s immediately after exercise
Measure arterial blood pressure after exercise
Measure pulse and pressure again at the end of the 3rd minute
⟦0⟧: the 10 s count is over — you should have counted the beats yourself.
First measure the pulse and pressure at rest
Release the air from the cuff
20 squats were completed in 30 s. Measure the pulse immediately, then the pressure!
First measure the pulse and pressure after exercise
The end of the 3rd minute has come (time was accelerated). Measure the pulse and pressure again.
Wait until the end of the 3rd minute
Counting the pulse: for 10 s a red dot lights up with every beat — count the beats yourself and multiply by 6. Measure the pressure by the Korotkoff method as before.
Did the values return to baseline at the end of the 3rd minute?
Normotonic (favorable): pulse increases by 50–75 %, systolic pressure rises by 15–30 mm, diastolic pressure stays the same or falls slightly, recovery within 3 minutes
Hypertonic (unfavorable): systolic pressure rises sharply (> 40–50 mm) and diastolic pressure rises too, recovery is slow
Hypotonic (asthenic, unfavorable): pulse accelerates sharply (> 100 %), pressure hardly changes, recovery is slow

In the normotonic response the load is met by a proportional increase in stroke volume and heart rate; dilation of arterioles in the working muscles keeps the diastolic pressure from rising. In the hypotonic response cardiac output increases mainly through heart rate (stroke volume does not increase) — the heart works uneconomically. The hypertonic response is typical of impaired vascular tone.
True values: pulse ⟦0⟧; pressure ⟦1⟧/⟦2⟧ → ⟦3⟧/⟦4⟧ → ⟦5⟧/⟦6⟧. Pulse increase ≈ ⟦7⟧ %.
Measuring lung volumes with a water spirometer
Tidal volume, ERV, VC, IRV, comparison with the predicted VC
has had curvature of the thoracic spine (kyphoscoliosis) since childhood, gets short of breath on stairs

Subject: ⟦0⟧-year-old ⟦1⟧, height ⟦2⟧ cm; ⟦3⟧. Task: determine the tidal volume, expiratory reserve volume (ERV), vital capacity (VC) and inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) with a water spirometer; compare the VC with the predicted value.
Wipe the mouthpiece with alcohol and put a clip on the nose
Tidal volume: after a quiet inspiration, exhale quietly into the spirometer 3 times
ERV: after a quiet expiration, exhale maximally into the spirometer
VC: inhale maximally and exhale maximally (3 times, the largest is taken)
Calculate the IRV, predicted VC and percentage
The mouthpiece was not wiped with alcohol
No nose clip — air escapes through the nose, so the result will be low
The mouthpiece was wiped with alcohol.
The nose clip was put on.
The valve was opened, the bell was lowered to zero and the valve was closed.
After a quiet inspiration, a quiet exhalation was made into the spirometer (attempt ⟦0⟧). Read the scale.
Maximal exhalation after a quiet exhalation (ERV)
The bell was not reset to zero — the previous air volume is added and the result will be wrong
After a quiet exhalation, a maximal exhalation was made into the spirometer. Read the scale.
The bell was not reset to zero — the VC must be measured from zero each time

The rise of the bell equals the volume of exhaled air. Scale: a small mark is 50 ml, the numbers are every 100 ml. Predicted VC (L) = (27.63 − 0.112 × age) × height (cm) / 1000 for men; (21.78 − 0.101 × age) × height / 1000 for women. Normally the actual VC is within ± 20 % of the predicted value.
VC (the largest of the three attempts)
Inspiratory reserve volume: IRV = VC − (TV + ERV)
Actual VC as a percentage of the predicted value
VC is within ± 20 % of the predicted value — external respiration is normal
VC is markedly below the predicted value (< 80 %) — lung expansion is limited (restrictive disorder)
VC is 50 % above the predicted value — obstructive disorder

VC = TV + IRV + ERV. In chest-wall deformity (kyphoscoliosis) and diseases of the pleura and lung tissue, lung expansion is limited — VC decreases (restrictive disorder). An obstructive disorder is detected during forced expiration (FEV₁, Tiffeneau index).
In this subject: TV attempts ⟦0⟧ ml; ERV ⟦1⟧ ml; VC attempts ⟦2⟧ ml; predicted VC ⟦3⟧ ml.

Normally air conduction is about 2 times longer than bone conduction (Rinne positive), and in the Weber test the sound is heard in the midline. When sound conduction is impaired (earwax plug, otitis), Rinne is negative in that ear and in the Weber test the sound lateralizes to the diseased ear. When sound perception is impaired (inner ear, auditory nerve), Rinne is positive but both conduction times are shortened; in the Weber test the sound lateralizes to the healthy ear.

Most of the reaction time is central delay — perceiving the signal, analyzing it and choosing the motor program. The simple reaction is normally ≈ 180–220 ms to light and ≈ 140–180 ms to sound (the auditory pathway is short and fast). The choice reaction requires discriminating two signals (differentiation) and inhibiting the response — the time lengthens; errors depend on the type of higher nervous activity, fatigue and attention.
